title: Jesus
summary: The New Testament presents Jesus through several kinds of writing. Matthew begins with his birth, Mark opens with the announcement of God’s kingdom, Luke shows Jesus reading Isaiah in Nazareth, and John calls him the Word who became flesh. Paul, Hebrews, and Colossians then interpret his self-giving, resurrection, and reign. Together these passages connect Jesus’ public story with claims about who he is and what his life means.
historical_context: Jesus lived in first-century Galilee and Judea under Roman rule within the world of Second Temple Judaism.
ancient_near_east_context: The Gospel scenes place Jesus in Jewish settings shaped by Scripture, synagogue worship, the Temple, and Roman rule. These institutions matter because the texts show Jesus teaching from Israel’s Scriptures and speaking about God’s reign within a lived community under imperial power. The references here are biblical texts, not comparative archaeological evidence for every practice of the period.
hebraic_worldview: The cited passages show Jesus’ story being told through Israel’s Scriptures and hopes. Luke 4 places him reading Isaiah in a synagogue and announcing fulfillment; Mark 1 connects his opening message with God’s kingdom; Matthew’s birth account places him within Israel’s story. These scenes help explain why the New Testament’s claims about Jesus use the language of promise, Messiah, and God’s reign.
second_temple_context: The Gospels portray Jesus as a Jewish teacher among Jewish communities: he reads Scripture in the synagogue, speaks within Israel’s prophetic hopes, and is associated with the Temple and its festivals. This setting helps readers hear his disputes and announcements as arguments within Jewish life of the period, rather than as detached religious abstractions. The passages do not make every Jewish group or teacher identical.
canonical_context: Within the New Testament, the accounts move from Jesus’ birth and public announcement to theological interpretation of his death and resurrection. John’s prologue calls him the Word made flesh; Philippians 2 describes his self-humbling and exaltation; Colossians 1 and Hebrews 1 speak of his relation to creation and God’s revelation; and 1 Corinthians 15 connects his resurrection with the future defeat of death. These passages explain how different New Testament writings connect the person in the Gospel narratives with the risen Lord they proclaim.
literary_context: The Gospels narrate Jesus’ life and teaching, while the letters and Revelation address communities that confess him after his death and resurrection. The selected passages make that shift visible: Luke 4 presents a public reading and announcement, John 1 offers a poetic opening, Philippians 2 uses a compact account of humility and exaltation, and 1 Corinthians 15 argues from resurrection toward the defeat of death. Reading each passage in its form keeps their different contributions clear.
covenantal_significance: These passages connect Jesus with Israel’s scriptural hopes and with the New Testament’s claims about forgiveness, resurrection, and God’s reign. Luke 4 presents his mission through Isaiah; Mark 1 announces God’s kingdom; and 1 Corinthians 15 describes his resurrection as the beginning of a future in which death is defeated. This explains why the New Testament treats Jesus as central to its account of redemption, while each passage contributes a distinct part of that account.
canonical_role: The climactic figure of the biblical storyline: incarnate Son, Messiah, mediator of the new covenant, crucified and risen Lord.

related_objects.notes: the reign of God proclaimed in his ministry

interpretive_notes.note: Hold together Jesus' humanity, deity, suffering, and reign; do not reduce him to a single role.
Read the Gospels and the rest of the New Testament as mutually interpreting witnesses to his identity.
